{{Short description|Theorem about right triangles}}
[[File:Hoehensatz2.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|area of grey square = area of grey rectangle: {{math|1= ''h''{{sup|2}} = ''pq'' ⟺ ''h'' = {{radic|''pq''}}}}]]

In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''right triangle altitude theorem''' or '''geometric mean theorem''' is a relation between the [[Altitude (triangle)|altitude]] on the [[hypotenuse]] in a [[right triangle]] and the two line segments it creates on the hypotenuse. It states that the [[geometric mean]] of those two segments equals the altitude.

==Theorem and its converse==
[[File:Sehnensatz hoehensatz.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|geometric mean theorem as a special case of the [[intersecting chords theorem]]: {{math|1= {{abs|''CD''}}{{abs|''DE''}} = {{abs|''AD''}}{{abs|''DB''}}}} {{math|1= ⟺ ''h''{{sup|2}} = ''pq''}}]]
If {{mvar|h}} denotes the altitude in a right triangle and {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} the segments on the hypotenuse then the theorem can be stated as:<ref name="HW"/>
<math display="block">h=\sqrt{pq} </math>
or in term of areas:
<math display="block">h^2=pq.</math>
The converse statement is true as well. Any triangle, in which the altitude equals the geometric mean of the two line segments created by it, is a right triangle.

The theorem can also be thought of as a special case of the [[intersecting chords theorem]] for a circle, since the converse of [[Thales' theorem]] ensures that the hypotenuse of the right angled triangle is the diameter of its [[circumcircle]].<ref name="HW"/>

== Applications ==
[[File:Root_construction_geometric_mean5.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Construction of {{math|{{radic|''p''}}}} by setting {{mvar|q}} to 1]]
[[File:Am gm half circle3.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Demonstration of [[AM–GM inequality]]]]
The formulation in terms of areas yields a method to square a rectangle with [[Compass and straightedge constructions|ruler and compass]], that is to construct a square of equal area to a given rectangle. For such a rectangle with sides {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} we denote its top left [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]] with {{mvar|D}} {{see below|{{slink|#Proof based on similarity}}, below, for a graphic of the construction}}. Now we extend the segment {{mvar|q}} to its left by {{mvar|p}} (using arc {{mvar|{{overline|AE}}}} centered on {{mvar|D}}) and draw a half circle with endpoints {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} with the new segment {{math|''p'' + ''q''}} as its diameter. Then we erect a perpendicular line to the diameter in {{mvar|D}} that intersects the half circle in {{mvar|C}}. Due to [[Thales' theorem]] {{mvar|C}} and the diameter form a [[right triangle]] with the line segment {{mvar|{{overline|DC}}}} as its altitude, hence {{mvar|{{overline|DC}}}} is the side of a square with the area of the rectangle. The method also allows for the construction of square roots (see [[constructible number]]), since starting with a rectangle that has a width of 1 the constructed square will have a side length that equals the square root of the rectangle's length.<ref name="HW">Hartmut Wellstein, Peter Kirsche: ''Elementargeometrie''. Springer, 2009, {{ISBN|9783834808561}}, pp. 76-77 (German, {{Google books|cFzWcl9xiGcC|online copy|page=76}})</ref>

Another application of this theorem provides a geometrical proof of the [[AM–GM inequality]] in the case of two numbers, since the half-circle's [[radius]] is the arithmetic mean of {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}}. This radius can be drawn parallel to the geometric mean constructed as above, which shows that geometric mean is always smaller or equal to the radius, and yields the inequality.<ref>Claudi Alsina, Roger B. Nelsen: ''[[Icons of Mathematics|Icons of Mathematics: An Exploration of Twenty Key Images]]''. MAA 2011, {{ISBN|9780883853528}}, pp.&nbsp;31–32 ({{Google books|4DavMl7-aFgC|online copy|page=31}})</ref>

== History ==
The theorem is usually attributed to [[Euclid]] (ca. 360–280 BC), who stated it as a corollary to proposition 8 in book VI of his [[Euclid's elements|Elements]]. In proposition 14 of book II Euclid gives a method for squaring a rectangle, which essentially matches the method given here. Euclid however provides a different slightly more complicated proof for the correctness of the construction rather than relying on the geometric mean theorem.<ref name="HW"/><ref>[[Euclid]]: [[Euclid's Elements|''Elements'']],  book II – prop. 14, book VI – prop. 8, ([http://aleph0.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/elements.html online copy])</ref>

==Proofs==
===Proof based on similarity===
[[File:Hoehensatz.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|{{center|{{math|△''ABC'' &sim; △''ADC'' &sim; △''DBC'' }}}}]]
====Proof of theorem====
The triangles {{math|△''ADC'' , △''BCD'' }} are [[Similar triangle#Similar triangles|similar]], since:
* consider triangles {{math|△''ABC'', △''ACD'' }}; here we have <math display=block>\angle ACB=\angle ADC=90^\circ, \quad \angle BAC=\angle CAD;</math> therefore by the [[AA postulate]] <math display=block>\triangle ABC \sim \triangle ACD .</math>
* further, consider triangles {{math|△''ABC'', △''BCD'' }}; here we have <math display=block>\angle ACB=\angle BDC= 90^\circ, \quad \angle ABC=\angle CBD;</math> therefore by the AA postulate <math display=block>\triangle ABC \sim \triangle BCD.</math>

Therefore, both triangles {{math|△''ACD'', △''BCD''}} are similar to {{math|△''ABC''}} and themselves, i.e. <math display=block>\triangle ACD \sim \triangle ABC \sim \triangle BCD.</math>

Because of the similarity we get the following equality of ratios and its algebraic rearrangement yields the theorem:<ref name="HW"/>
<math display="block"> \frac{h}{p}=\frac{q}{h}\,\iff\,h^2=pq\,\iff\,h=\sqrt{pq}\qquad (h,p,q> 0)</math>

====Proof of converse====
For the converse we have a triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} in which {{math|1=''h''{{sup|2}} = ''pq''}} holds and need to show that the angle at {{mvar|C}} is a right angle. Now because of {{math|1=''h''{{sup|2}} = ''pq''}} we also have <math>\tfrac{h}{p}=\tfrac{q}{h}.</math> Together with <math>\angle ADC=\angle CDB </math> the triangles {{math|△''ADC'', △''BDC''}} have an angle of equal size and have corresponding pairs of legs with the same ratio. This means the triangles are similar, which yields:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\angle ACB &= \angle ACD +\angle DCB \\
           &= \angle ACD+(90^\circ-\angle DBC) \\
           &= \angle ACD+(90^\circ-\angle ACD) \\
           &= 90^\circ
\end{align}</math>

===Proof based on the Pythagorean theorem===
[[File:Hoehensatz beweis pythagoras.svg|thumb|upright=1.0|Proof with the Pythagorean theorem]]
In the setting of the geometric mean theorem there are three right triangles {{math|△''ABC''}}, {{math|△''ADC''}} and {{math|△''DBC''}} in which the Pythagorean theorem yields:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
h^2 &= a^2-q^2 \\
h^2 &= b^2-p^2 \\
c^2 &= a^2+b^2
\end{align}</math>
Adding the first 2 two equations and then using the third then leads to:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
2h^2 &= a^2+b^2-p^2-q^2 \\
     &= c^2-p^2-q^2 \\
     &= (p+q)^2-p^2-q^2 \\
     &= 2pq \\
\therefore \ h^2 &= pq,
\end{align}</math>
which finally yields the formula of the geometric mean theorem.<ref>[[Ilka Agricola]], Thomas Friedrich: ''Elementary Geometry''. AMS 2008, {{ISBN|9780821843475}}, p.&nbsp;25  ({{Google books|LLXxBwAAQBAJ|online copy|page=25}}) </ref>

===Proof based on dissection and rearrangement===
[[File:Geometrischer Höhensatzbeweis.svg]]

Dissecting the right triangle along its altitude {{mvar|h}} yields two similar triangles, which can be augmented and arranged in two alternative ways into a larger right triangle with perpendicular sides of lengths {{math|''p'' + ''h''}} and {{math|''q'' + ''h''}}. One such arrangement requires a square of area {{math|''h''{{sup|2}}}} to complete it, the other a rectangle of area {{mvar|pq}}. Since both arrangements yield the same triangle, the areas of the square and the rectangle must be identical.

===Proof based on shear mappings===
A square constructed on the altitude can be transformed into a rectangle of equal area with sides {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} with the help of three [[shear mapping]]s (shear mappings preserve the area):
[[File:Scherungen alle2.svg|thumb|center|upright=4.0|Shear mappings with their associated fixed lines (dotted), starting with the original square as preimage each parallelogram displays the image of a shear mapping of the figure left of it]]
